title: Bombay High Court Denies Relief to Thane Eatery Caught Serving Analogue Paneer
excerpt: A bench led by Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge refused to stay the FDA's licence suspension of Udupi Swaad restaurant, directing it to appeal before the Commissioner of Food Safety.
body:
• The Bombay High Court has refused interim relief to Udupi Swaad restaurant in Thane, whose food licence was suspended by the Maharashtra FDA after lab tests found foreign fat in its paneer.
  • A division bench led by Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge told the eatery it must "suffer for sometime," calling it "poetic justice" for making customers suffer.
  • The court directed the restaurant to appeal before the Commissioner of Food Safety and questioned whether it had ever disclosed to customers that the paneer was not dairy.
  • Maharashtra has banned analogue paneer for one year under a notification by FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, amid a wider national crackdown on non-dairy substitutes.

The Bombay High Court has refused to grant interim relief to a Thane restaurant whose food licence was suspended after government laboratory tests found that the "paneer" it served was actually a cheese analogue containing non-dairy fat. A division bench of Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge and Justice Gautam Ankhad directed M/s Udupi Swaad Restaurant to pursue its appeal before the Commissioner of Food Safety instead, delivering a pointed rebuke on consumer trust.

"Let the FDA reply come, suffer till then. You also need to suffer first as you have made people suffer by eating this. Poetic justice!"

— Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge, Bombay High Court

Food safety officers from the FDA's Thane division had collected a sample of loose paneer from the restaurant in Thane's Wagle Estate. According to the government laboratory report, the sample contained foreign fat instead of dairy-based ingredients and was declared "unsafe" under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The subsequent investigation found the restaurant was allegedly purchasing a cheese analogue in the name of paneer and using it in dishes sold to customers as paneer-based products — without any prior disclosure.

Disclosure, or the lack of it

The bench's sharpest questions went to the heart of consumer rights. "Have you advertised in your menu card or indicated to customers that you are serving them analogue paneer and not the actual paneer?" the judges asked. "Why don't you advertise on your signboard that original food is not available with you?" When Additional Government Pleader Priyabhushan Kakade told the court the samples showed oil mixed with chemicals in place of dairy, the bench asked: "Just for little price difference, you do this?"

The restaurant argued that the FDA should have issued a mandatory improvement notice under the Food Safety and Standards Act before suspending its licence, and pointed to severe revenue and reputation losses from the abrupt closure. It also noted that the state's ban on analogue paneer was notified on August 1, while the paneer in question was found in the establishment in June. The court was unmoved, telling the petitioner it could not claim unfair treatment when the alleged violation involved serving an ingredient customers had never been told about. The judges also observed that customers served such food may have grounds to seek compensation.

A wider war on fake paneer

The case sits inside a much larger enforcement drive. Maharashtra's FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has prohibited the sale and use of analogue paneer across the state for one year, and the crackdown has since spread to multiple states and drawn the attention of the National Human Rights Commission. Analogue paneer — made from vegetable oils and emulsifiers rather than milk — has quietly infiltrated restaurants, cloud kitchens and catering services, exploiting the price gap between dairy and synthetic substitutes.

The FDA's action in Thane is part of that pattern: officials say the practice of passing off substitutes without disclosure poses a potential risk to public health, and the laboratory's "unsafe" declaration gave the designated officer grounds for immediate licence suspension.

Diaspora kitchens take note

The analogue-paneer problem is not confined to India. Non-dairy paneer substitutes are sold openly in diaspora grocery aisles in the US, UK and Canada, where labelling rules vary and restaurant supply chains are harder to trace. The Bombay High Court's ruling is a reminder that when a customer orders paneer, the law expects milk — and the burden of disclosure sits squarely with the seller.

What's next

The restaurant must now take its appeal to the Commissioner of Food Safety, the alternate remedy the court pointed it toward. The FDA, meanwhile, has signalled no let-up: licence actions against establishments using undisclosed substitutes will continue, and officials say the one-year state ban gives them room to pursue prosecutions where lab reports confirm adulteration.
